title: SAVE America Act is all the rage this week, the House passed it, the Senate is deliberating it,…
text:
SAVE America Act is all the rage this week, the House passed it, the Senate is deliberating it, with the Prez encouraging dissolution of the Filibuster Rule to bypass the 60-vote threshold (which cannot be reached in this divided Senate). The potential consequences are massive (unintended).  Get your popcorn...

As the WSJ EB points out, voter fraud is exceedingly rare, as is the issue of non-citizens casting votes. States and counties already have methods of identifying people who aren't eligible.  This bill is a solution in search of a problem that will only succeed in disenfranchising tens of millions of American citizens in return for negligible improvements in election security.   

Time for the Editorial Board to, again, ignore the elephant in the room that is Donald Trump's extensive attempts to overturn an election that he lost. It's extremely silly to discuss this bill without that extremely important context.

Acknowledging that would require acknowledging that they support a vile and malignant anti-democratic demagogue and aberration from political norms.

It's much easier to sleep at night if you pretend that he is a normal politician with mean tweets and that this is a normal election bill.

title: There are a pair of articles pertaining to health in today's NY Times that require attention.
text:
There are a pair of articles pertaining to health in today's NY Times that require attention. One is regarding Rubio's attempt to negotiate HIV aid to Zambia in return for access to the country's rare earth minerals and other negotiations.  The other is the MA court pushback against RFKs vaccine agenda (suit brought by major medical organizations such as the Peds Society and the Thoracic Society, AMA, and others).

Zambia issue crystallizes the approach Trump 2.0 has taken to all issues, global and domestic, that is largely transactional based on "who holds the cards", economic strength dictates terms, and military might is right.  Where you fall on this approach largely depends on your values, your world view, and how you view human interactions.  One view could be based on winners and losers, you got your advantages by sheer merit (not by many other variables), and that we are in an existential battle for survival in a jungle and we must have the upper hand.  Of course, there are other ways to approach conflict.  Those may be viewed as being weak, for suckers, etc.

I know where I stand on this issue of PEPFAR, Zambia, and AIDS drugs.  We live in a connected world, and I firmly believe that good works is the way for global health.

The second article is the continuing battle to constrain the dismantling of public health by RFK, et al.

text: Sarasota has a strong live jazz scene, to my surprise! it really is a great arts town! The jazz society is active at multiple venues throughout the winter season (for the snowbirds). title: I try not to be "conspiratorial." But I found this episode of the NY Times Daily by 2 noted…
text:
I try not to be "conspiratorial."  But I found this episode of the NY Times Daily by 2 noted journalists to be disturbing on many levels, of the intertwining of US foreign policy so closely with Israel, in a very complex and combustible middle east. Many of the neighbors are pursuing modernity with thriving economies, are being pulled into an expanding regional conflict. Israel's domestic interests are not identical to US interests or global interests. Hopefully, this is not too controversial.

The U.S. decision to strike Iran was a victory for Israel, which had been pushing President Trump for months on the need to hit the country. Now, Israel’s role in spurring the operation has become a point of political tension. The New York Times journalists Mark Mazzetti and Ronen Bergman discuss what we know about the extraordinarily close cooperation between Israel and the United States. Guest: Mark Mazzetti, an investigative reporter for The New York Times in Washington, D.C., focusing on national security. Ronen Bergman, a staff writer for The New York Times Magazine in Tel Aviv. 
Background reading:  How Mr. Trump decided to go to war. Photo: Tierney L. Cross/The New York Times For more information on today’s episode, visit nytimes.com/the daily.

title: As we try to understand the current Israeli / US bombing of Iran, it is important to keep in…
text:
As we try to understand the current Israeli / US bombing of Iran, it is important to keep in context the much bigger global chess game behind the scenes. The existential positioning is the rivalry between the US and China, everyone else is a pawn or bit player.  China is a major importer of oil from both Iran and Venezuela. Oil and LNG are important, and the US has the upper hand (with shale oil surplus) till the alternate fuel technologies catch up, hence the efforts to corner and capture Venezuela and Iran.  Everything else is noise!

P.s. clarification: China accounts for 85-90% of oil exports from Iran and Venezuela; but, China's overall oil needs are so large, they only comprise <20% of their consumption.  So how critical is this component?

title: I found this discussion interesting and did not realize there was a Buddhist thought or…
text:
I found this discussion interesting and did not realize there was a Buddhist thought or tradition in the AA community.  Applying that to James Baldwin's thought is provocative. This discussion of anger vs. hate is clarifying, the former being energizing whereas the latter is an ossified pattern that is corrosive to self and not constructive.  

I find Liz Bucar a provocative and thoughtful progressive voice, though I do not share ALL her views!

Post-script:

I just "audio-read" this book by Rima Flad.  I

Fire Inside is a memoir-inflected reflection on trauma, resilience, racism in America, and self-reconstruction. Rima Flad traces her journey through personal upheaval—family dysfunction, emotional injury, cultural expectations, and identity conflict—toward psychological and spiritual reclamation. The “fire” of the title functions as a dual metaphor: destructive suffering and catalytic transformation.

Importantly, Rima Flad invokes James Baldwin and Audre Lorde as moral and intellectual touchstones rather than subjects of formal literary analysis. Her engagement with both writers centers on their shared insistence that confronting inner truth is inseparable from confronting social reality.

The book blends narrative storytelling with therapeutic insight. Flad recounts formative experiences—moments of betrayal, dislocation, anger, and self-doubt—while exploring how suppressed emotion calcifies into shame and how confrontation of pain can become a generative force. She frames healing as an active process: reclaiming agency, naming wounds, setting boundaries, and redefining selfhood beyond inherited scripts.

Ultimately, Fire Inside argues that adversity, when consciously metabolized, becomes fuel. The memoir closes on a note of hard-won empowerment: identity not as something given but forged.

ð¥ On James Baldwin

Flad draws on Baldwin’s idea that self-deception is a national and personal disease. She echoes his argument that refusing to face historical and emotional truth perpetuates suffering. From Baldwin, she adopts:

The courage to interrogate one’s own complicity in inherited narratives.

The belief that rage, when clarified rather than denied, can become moral clarity.

The conviction that identity must be wrestled with, not passively accepted.

In her reading, Baldwin models intellectual bravery—the refusal to look away from injustice or internal contradiction.

ð On Audre Lorde

From Lorde, Flad emphasizes the transformative potential of anger and difference. She aligns particularly with Lorde’s assertion that silence does not protect. Lorde’s framing of anger as information—not pathology—resonates strongly with Flad’s own journey of reclaiming suppressed emotion.

Key themes she draws from Lorde:

Anger as a catalyst for self-definition.

The political dimension of personal pain.

The necessity of speaking from one’s lived experience, even when uncomfortable.

ð§­ How Flad Synthesizes Them

Flad uses Baldwin and Lorde less as literary subjects and more as ethical guides. Baldwin offers the discipline of truth-telling; Lorde offers the permission to feel and voice what has been silenced. Together, they reinforce her central thesis: the “fire inside” is not merely private anguish—it is a force that can illuminate systems, relationships, and inherited constraints.

Her treatment is reverential but selective—she focuses on the themes that align with her memoir’s arc rather than offering a comprehensive critique of either thinker.

Overall, I found parts of her Black Buddhist tradition, approach to an unjust world and personal rage, and channeling it to activism to be inspiring. In that sense, I learned a lot, including her interpretation of her intellectual muses. She contextualizes that to her views on the current Palestinian plight and her deep anger towards the crisis, yet with continuing sympathy towards Jews.  This made sense.  However, her narrative is overly "whining" about her grandparents' racism (they were white and ashamed of a dark-skinned granddaughter) and was off-putting to me. Also, the discussion of lesbian feminism in the last chapter did not connect with me or will it for a broader audience. I would recommend this to a niche audience.

title: This is an outstanding episode on healthcare and AI, with Dr.
text:
This is an outstanding episode on healthcare and AI, with Dr. Robert Wachter, Chair of Medicine at UCSF. He reviews the changes in healthcare from recent widespread deployment of the electronic medical record with Epic as the dominant player. The very recent use of "ambient medical scribe" to auto generate a physician note on a clinical encounter or summarize a large chart by an LLM prior to a patient visit.  And the emergent applications for early detection of disease, such as using the rudimentary EKG to predict structural heart disease and the need for an echo study.  The diagnostics and decision support will rapidly transform the industry.  Interestingly, Wachter indicates that the near monopoly of a proprietary EMR Epic is a major hurdle for applying AI to medical records and attempts to circumvent that.

I highly recommend this to my healthcare colleagues, as this space is evolving rapidly.

Also, check out this book review of The Great Leap, by Wachter

https://www.wsj.com/arts-culture/books/a-giant-leap-review-disruption-for-doctors-4466ef18?st=Rs3W89&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink

title: In this age of free flowing "information", credibility and trust matters as does the source of…
text:
In this age of free flowing "information", credibility and trust matters as does the source of information. The highest levels of government, which has the greatest means and tools, has an exceptional obligation to navigate truth carefully and accurately. When the responsible officials (Noem, Patel, Bovino) are more interested in a PR campaign to make themselves look good and actively resist prima facie evidence or an investigation, there is a breakdown of confidence (and a call to action by onlookers such as myself to bear witness). 
At present, I do not trust what is coming out from those in power about Minneapolis (or many other issues for that matter), a sad state.

title: Just listened to The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, by Douglas Adams (1979, the first book of…
text:
Just listened to The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, by Douglas Adams (1979, the first book of a series).  I see this book being referenced often as dystopian. I first came across it in the Elon Musk biography by Walter Isaacson (apparently this was very influential on Musk!).  

The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy is a sci-fi comedy that treats the universe as vast, absurd, and deeply indifferent—then laughs at it anyway.  Initially was a BBC Radio series that was adapted to many formats with a cult following.

The story begins when Arthur Dent, an utterly ordinary Englishman, discovers that Earth is about to be demolished to make way for an interstellar hyperspace bypass. He’s saved at the last second by Ford Prefect, who turns out not to be from Guildford but an alien researcher for a galactic travel book called The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy (whose most important advice is: “Don’t Panic.”)

As Earth is vaporized, Arthur is swept into space and joins a cast of gloriously dysfunctional characters:

Zaphod Beeblebrox, a two-headed, semi-insane galactic president

Trillian, a human who left Earth earlier and actually adapted

Marvin, a robot with a brain the size of a planet and crippling depression

They travel aboard the Heart of Gold, a spaceship powered by the Infinite Improbability Drive, which allows literally anything—however unlikely—to happen.

Along the way, the novel skewers bureaucracy, technology, philosophy, and humanity’s need for meaning. The book’s most famous revelation—that the Answer to the Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe, and Everything is 42—perfectly captures Adams’s core joke: the universe may have answers, but they’re useless without the right questions.

What it’s really about

The absurdity of existence

The futility (and comedy) of seeking cosmic meaning

Satire of politics, science, religion, and human self-importance

Why towels are the most important item you can carry

Tone

Fast, irreverent, philosophical, British, and relentlessly funny—less about plot than about ideas and punchlines that sneak up on you.

Key one-liners from the book:

ð Existential / Cosmic Absurdity

“The Answer to the Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe, and Everything isâ¦ 42.”

“Space is big. Really big.”

“In the beginning the Universe was created. This has made a lot of people very angry and been widely regarded as a bad move.”

ð¤ Technology & Bureaucracy

“A common mistake that people make when trying to design something completely foolproof is to underestimate the ingenuity of complete fools.”

“The ships hung in the sky in much the same way that bricks don’t.”

“It is a mistake to think you can solve any major problems just with potatoes.”

ð§  Philosophy, Adams-style

“If you think you’re sane, you probably aren’t.”

“Anyone who is capable of getting themselves made President should on no account be allowed to do the job.”

“Human beings, who are almost unique in having the ability to learn from the experience of others, are also remarkable for their apparent disinclination to do so.”

ð Marvin (existential despair perfected)

“I’ve got this terrible pain in all the diodes down my left side.”

“Life. Don’t talk to me about life.”

“I think you ought to know I’m feeling very depressed.”

Just listened to The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, by Douglas Adams (1979, the first book of a series).  I see this book being referenced often as dystopian. I first came across it in the Elon Musk biography by Walter Isaacson (apparently this was very influential on Musk!).  

The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy is a sci-fi comedy that treats the universe as vast, absurd, and deeply indifferent—then laughs at it anyway.  Initially was a BBC Radio series that was adapted to many formats with a cult following.

The story begins when Arthur Dent, an utterly ordinary Englishman, discovers that Earth is about to be demolished to make way for an interstellar hyperspace bypass. He’s saved at the last second by Ford Prefect, who turns out not to be from Guildford but an alien researcher for a galactic travel book called The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy (whose most important advice is: “Don’t Panic.”)

As Earth is vaporized, Arthur is swept into space and joins a cast of gloriously dysfunctional characters:

Zaphod Beeblebrox, a two-headed, semi-insane galactic president

Trillian, a human who left Earth earlier and actually adapted

Marvin, a robot with a brain the size of a planet and crippling depression

They travel aboard the Heart of Gold, a spaceship powered by the Infinite Improbability Drive, which allows literally anything—however unlikely—to happen.

Along the way, the novel skewers bureaucracy, technology, philosophy, and humanity’s need for meaning. The book’s most famous revelation—that the Answer to the Ultimate Question of Life, the Universe, and Everything is 42—perfectly captures Adams’s core joke: the universe may have answers, but they’re useless without the right questions.

What it’s really about

The absurdity of existence

The futility (and comedy) of seeking cosmic meaning

Satire of politics, science, religion, and human self-importance

Why towels are the most important item you can carry

Tone

Fast, irreverent, philosophical, British, and relentlessly funny—less about plot than about ideas and punchlines that sneak up on you.

“The ships hung in the sky in much the same way that bricks don’t.”

“It is a mistake to think you can solve any major problems just with potatoes.”

ð§  Philosophy, Adams-style

“Anyone who is capable of getting themselves made President should on no account be allowed to do the job.”

“Human beings, who are almost unique in having the ability to learn from the experience of others, are also remarkable for their apparent disinclination to do so.”

title: This is not a new topic, but the impact of "therapy culture" caught my attention!
text:
This is not a new topic, but the impact of "therapy culture" caught my attention!

The Atlantic article “A Shift in American Family Values Is Fueling Estrangement” by Joshua Coleman, published in 2021, explores the rising phenomenon of family estrangement in the United States, particularly between parents and their adult children. Coleman, a psychologist and author specializing in family dynamics, argues that this trend stems from evolving cultural and societal values over the past 50 years, which have reshaped expectations and norms within families. Below is a detailed summary of the article’s key points, arguments, and insights.

Key Themes and Arguments

Changing Family Dynamics and Cultural Shifts:

Coleman highlights that the “rules” of family life have transformed significantly since the mid-20th century. Previously, family relationships were governed by duty, obligation, and hierarchical structures, with parents holding more authority. Today, family ties are increasingly defined by individual choice, emotional satisfaction, and mutual respect.
This shift is rooted in broader societal changes, including the rise of individualism, the influence of therapy culture, and evolving notions of personal identity. Adult children now prioritize their own mental health and personal fulfillment, sometimes leading to estrangement when family relationships are perceived as toxic or unfulfilling.

The Role of Individualism:

The article emphasizes that American culture has become more individualistic, prioritizing personal happiness and self-actualization over collective family loyalty. This contrasts with earlier generations, where enduring familial conflict or maintaining contact despite disagreements was more common.
Adult children are more likely to cut ties with parents if they feel their emotional needs are not met or if they perceive their parents’ behavior as harmful, controlling, or dismissive of their identity (e.g., conflicts over sexuality, politics, or lifestyle choices).

Therapy Culture and Psychological Frameworks:

Coleman notes the influence of therapy and psychological concepts in shaping modern family dynamics. Terms like “boundaries,” “toxicity,” and “trauma” have become mainstream, empowering individuals to set limits on relationships, including with family members.
While therapy can foster self-awareness and healing, it can also lead to estrangement when adult children reinterpret past parental behaviors through a modern psychological lens, sometimes viewing them as abusive or neglectful, even if those actions were normative in earlier eras.

Parental Perspectives and Misunderstandings:

Parents often struggle to understand why their adult children distance themselves, as their parenting was shaped by the norms of their time (e.g., stricter discipline or less emotional openness). Coleman shares anecdotes from his practice, where parents feel blindsided by estrangement, often unaware of how their actions were perceived.
For example, parents may see their past efforts (e.g., providing for the family) as sufficient proof of love, while adult children may prioritize emotional connection or acknowledgment of past grievances.

The Impact of Technology and Social Media:

Technology plays a role in estrangement by enabling adult children to maintain distance more easily (e.g., blocking parents on social media or moving far away). It also amplifies exposure to alternative viewpoints, such as online communities that encourage cutting off “toxic” family members.
Conversely, social media can exacerbate conflicts by publicizing private disputes or highlighting ideological differences (e.g., political disagreements during polarized times).

Generational Differences in Expectations:

Coleman points out a generational gap in expectations. Older generations often view family ties as permanent and obligatory, while younger generations see them as conditional, based on mutual respect and compatibility.
This mismatch can lead to hurt feelings, as parents may expect unwavering loyalty, while adult children feel justified in setting boundaries or cutting contact to protect their well-being.

The Pain and Consequences of Estrangement:

Estrangement is often deeply painful for both sides. Parents may experience grief, guilt, or shame, while adult children may feel relief but also loss or unresolved anger.
Coleman notes that estrangement is not always permanent, but reconciliation requires both parties to acknowledge the other’s perspective and adapt to new family norms. However, the article suggests that cultural emphasis on individual choice makes reconciliation less likely in some cases.

Societal and Economic Factors:

The article touches on how economic pressures, such as the rising cost of living and geographic mobility, contribute to estrangement. Adult children may move far from their parents, reducing opportunities for in-person connection and making misunderstandings harder to resolve.
Additionally, societal polarization (e.g., over politics or cultural issues) can deepen family rifts, as differing values become harder to bridge.

Case Studies and Examples
Coleman weaves in real-life examples from his practice to illustrate the complexity of estrangement:

A mother is estranged from her daughter after criticizing her lifestyle choices, unaware that her comments were perceived as judgmental and controlling.
A father struggles to reconnect with his son, who cut contact after the father dismissed his son’s mental health struggles, reflecting a generational gap in understanding mental health.
These cases underscore how misunderstandings and differing expectations can escalate into full estrangement.

Solutions and Reflections

Coleman advocates for empathy and communication to bridge the gap. He encourages parents to listen to their children’s grievances without defensiveness and to apologize when appropriate, even if they don’t fully agree with the child’s perspective.
For adult children, he suggests reflecting on whether estrangement is truly necessary or if less drastic boundaries could suffice. He acknowledges, however, that some relationships may be too damaging to maintain.
He also calls for a broader cultural conversation about balancing individual needs with family obligations, suggesting that society’s emphasis on personal happiness may need tempering with an appreciation for enduring family ties.

Broader Implications

The article frames estrangement as a symptom of larger cultural shifts, including the decline of traditional family structures, the rise of mental health awareness, and the impact of societal polarization. Coleman argues that while these changes empower individuals, they also risk fraying familial bonds, potentially leading to increased isolation and loss of intergenerational support.

Conclusion

Coleman concludes that estrangement reflects a profound transformation in American family values, driven by individualism, therapy culture, and changing social norms. While these shifts offer greater personal freedom, they also challenge traditional notions of family loyalty and obligation. The article calls for mutual understanding and adaptation to navigate these new dynamics, recognizing that both parents and adult children must grapple with the emotional and cultural complexities of modern family life.
Notes

The article relies on Coleman’s professional experience and anecdotal evidence. It focuses primarily on parent-adult child estrangement, with less emphasis on sibling or other family estrangements. Coleman’s tone is empathetic to both parents and children, avoiding judgment while highlighting the challenges of reconciling differing generational perspectives.

Prevalence of Estrangement:

A 2023 study by Rin Reczek and colleagues, published in the Journal of Marriage and Family, found that 26% of adult children reported estrangement from their fathers, while 6% reported estrangement from their mothers, based on data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979 (1979â2018). This indicates adult children are over four times more likely to be estranged from fathers than mothers.

A 2024 survey by Joshua Coleman and Will Johnson, reported in TIME, found that 1 in 2 American adults (50%) are estranged from a close relative, with 1 in 5 (20%) citing political differences as the primary reason. Nearly half of these estrangements occurred within the past year, with 1 in 7 happening in the month leading up to the 2024 election.

Karl Pillemer’s 2020 study, cited in Fault Lines: Fractured Families and How to Mend Them, reported that 27% of Americans are estranged from a family member, translating to roughly 67 million people.

A 2025 YouGov poll indicated that 16% of U.S. adult citizens are currently estranged from a parent, and 38% are estranged from at least one family member (e.g., sibling, parent, child, grandparent, or grandchild).

Demographic Variations:

Gender: Daughters are 22% more likely than sons to be estranged from their fathers but slightly less likely to be estranged from their mothers. Black adult children are 27% less likely to be estranged from their mothers than White adult children, but Black and Latino adults are more likely to be estranged from their fathers compared to White adults.

Sexuality: Gay and lesbian adult children are 86% more likely to be estranged from their fathers than heterosexuals, while bisexuals are nearly three times as likely. No significant differences were found in estrangement from mothers based on sexuality.

Age: Estrangement often begins in early adulthood, with the average age of first estrangement from mothers at 26 and from fathers at 23. Younger adults (under 35) are more likely to report estrangement due to political differences.

Divorce: Over 70% of estranged parents surveyed by Joshua Coleman had divorced their child’s other parent, with children of divorce more likely to estrange from fathers. Divorce increases the likelihood of estrangement due to factors like parental alienation or family fragmentation.

Reasons for Estrangement:

A 2015 study by Lucy Blake found that 77% of adult children cited emotional abuse as the reason for estrangement from mothers, and 59% for fathers. A 2025 YouGov poll noted that 34% of those estranged from a parent cited manipulative behavior, and 26% cited personality conflicts.
Other common reasons include differing values, emotional disconnection, overbearing relationships, and unmet emotional needs, with political differences playing a significant role in recent years.

Reconciliation Trends:

The Reczek study found that 81% of estrangements with mothers and 69% with fathers eventually end, suggesting many estrangements are temporary.
However, the YouGov poll indicated that 39% of those estranged from a parent say there are no circumstances under which they would consider reconciling, while 35% are open to reconciliation under certain conditions.

Cultural and Temporal Context:

Estrangement is more socially accepted today due to shifts toward individualism and mental health awareness. Over 1 in 4 families (27%) experience some form of estrangement, with onset typically around age 25.
Political polarization, particularly post-2016, has intensified estrangements, with 1 in 5 estrangements directly tied to political differences in the 2024 survey.

Notes:

Data varies due to differences in study design (e.g., sample size, definitions of estrangement). For example, Reczek’s study used longitudinal data, while Coleman’s survey focused on recent political impacts.
The lack of consensus on prevalence reflects challenges in defining and reporting estrangement, as it is often underreported due to stigma.

These statistics align with the themes in Joshua Coleman’s Atlantic article, which emphasizes cultural shifts toward individualism and therapy culture as drivers of estrangement.

Broader Implications

The article frames estrangement as a symptom of larger cultural shifts, including the decline of traditional family structures, the rise of mental health awareness, and the impact of societal polarization. Coleman argues that while these changes empower individuals, they also risk fraying familial bonds, potentially leading to increased isolation and loss of intergenerational support.

Conclusion

Coleman concludes that estrangement reflects a profound transformation in American family values, driven by individualism, therapy culture, and changing social norms. While these shifts offer greater personal freedom, they also challenge traditional notions of family loyalty and obligation. The article calls for mutual understanding and adaptation to navigate these new dynamics, recognizing that both parents and adult children must grapple with the emotional and cultural complexities of modern family life.
Notes

The article relies on Coleman’s professional experience and anecdotal evidence. It focuses primarily on parent-adult child estrangement, with less emphasis on sibling or other family estrangements. Coleman’s tone is empathetic to both parents and children, avoiding judgment while highlighting the challenges of reconciling differing generational perspectives.

Prevalence of Estrangement:

A 2023 study by Rin Reczek and colleagues, published in the Journal of Marriage and Family, found that 26% of adult children reported estrangement from their fathers, while 6% reported estrangement from their mothers, based on data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1979 (1979â2018). This indicates adult children are over four times more likely to be estranged from fathers than mothers.

A 2024 survey by Joshua Coleman and Will Johnson, reported in TIME, found that 1 in 2 American adults (50%) are estranged from a close relative, with 1 in 5 (20%) citing political differences as the primary reason. Nearly half of these estrangements occurred within the past year, with 1 in 7 happening in the month leading up to the 2024 election.

Karl Pillemer’s 2020 study, cited in Fault Lines: Fractured Families and How to Mend Them, reported that 27% of Americans are estranged from a family member, translating to roughly 67 million people.

A 2025 YouGov poll indicated that 16% of U.S. adult citizens are currently estranged from a parent, and 38% are estranged from at least one family member (e.g., sibling, parent, child, grandparent, or grandchild).

Demographic Variations:

Gender: Daughters are 22% more likely than sons to be estranged from their fathers but slightly less likely to be estranged from their mothers. Black adult children are 27% less likely to be estranged from their mothers than White adult children, but Black and Latino adults are more likely to be estranged from their fathers compared to White adults.

Sexuality: Gay and lesbian adult children are 86% more likely to be estranged from their fathers than heterosexuals, while bisexuals are nearly three times as likely. No significant differences were found in estrangement from mothers based on sexuality.

Age: Estrangement often begins in early adulthood, with the average age of first estrangement from mothers at 26 and from fathers at 23. Younger adults (under 35) are more likely to report estrangement due to political differences.

Divorce: Over 70% of estranged parents surveyed by Joshua Coleman had divorced their child’s other parent, with children of divorce more likely to estrange from fathers. Divorce increases the likelihood of estrangement due to factors like parental alienation or family fragmentation.

Reasons for Estrangement:

A 2015 study by Lucy Blake found that 77% of adult children cited emotional abuse as the reason for estrangement from mothers, and 59% for fathers. A 2025 YouGov poll noted that 34% of those estranged from a parent cited manipulative behavior, and 26% cited personality conflicts.
Other common reasons include differing values, emotional disconnection, overbearing relationships, and unmet emotional needs, with political differences playing a significant role in recent years.

Reconciliation Trends:

The Reczek study found that 81% of estrangements with mothers and 69% with fathers eventually end, suggesting many estrangements are temporary.
However, the YouGov poll indicated that 39% of those estranged from a parent say there are no circumstances under which they would consider reconciling, while 35% are open to reconciliation under certain conditions.

Cultural and Temporal Context:

Estrangement is more socially accepted today due to shifts toward individualism and mental health awareness. Over 1 in 4 families (27%) experience some form of estrangement, with onset typically around age 25.
Political polarization, particularly post-2016, has intensified estrangements, with 1 in 5 estrangements directly tied to political differences in the 2024 survey.

Notes:

Data varies due to differences in study design (e.g., sample size, definitions of estrangement). For example, Reczek’s study used longitudinal data, while Coleman’s survey focused on recent political impacts.
The lack of consensus on prevalence reflects challenges in defining and reporting estrangement, as it is often underreported due to stigma.

These statistics align with the themes in Joshua Coleman’s Atlantic article, which emphasizes cultural shifts toward individualism and therapy culture as drivers of estrangement.
